steps.title: What an operating system does
steps.content: An operating system manages hardware and provides services for programs. Core responsibilities include process management, memory management, files, devices, security and scheduling.
steps.example: When you open a browser, the OS creates or schedules processes and manages memory and device access.

steps.title: Process versus program
options: A program stored on disk only
steps.explanation: A process is an executing instance of a program with its own execution state and resources.

steps.title: Process scheduling
steps.content: The scheduler decides which ready process receives CPU time. Context switching saves one process's state and loads another's. Switching has overhead, so it is not free.
steps.tip: A process is a running program; a thread is an execution path within a process.

steps.title: Understand deadlock
steps.prompt: Which condition is one of the classic necessary conditions for deadlock?
steps.explanation: The four Coffman conditions include mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait.

steps.title: Virtual memory
steps.content: Virtual memory gives each process a virtual address space. The OS and hardware translate virtual addresses to physical memory; pages may be loaded on demand.
steps.example: A page fault occurs when a referenced page is not currently mapped in physical memory and must be resolved.

questions.prompt: Which is a core operating-system responsibility?
questions.explanation: The OS manages memory resources for processes.

questions.explanation: The CPU switches execution by saving one state and restoring another.

questions.explanation: The four conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait.

questions.explanation: The memory system must resolve a reference to a page that is not currently resident.
